extracted.intended_audience: general readers / comedy fans / documentary viewers interested in Tig Notaro and personal-story comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and implicit lessons about crafting and performing personal-story comedy (standup and documentary) drawn from Tig Notaro's Largo set and the Netflix documentary 'Tig'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutal honesty / candid storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece describes Notaro's Largo set as a "brutally honest set" that "catapulted her career," implying candid, unvarnished personal truth is a key quality in powerful comedic storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: the Largo performance recounted personal tragedies and cancer diagnosis; Louis CK distributed a recording and social media amplified it. Example/implication: telling raw, honest truth onstage can create career-changing impact. Anti-pattern: sanitizing or disguising the core truth so the material loses its emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience fit and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Success depended on the specific audience: "those were the exact, perfect people in that show" who made Notaro feel, "Wow, they really are with me."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: the show was "very up and down," with belly laughs and people crying; a mid-show shout of "This is f**king amazing" and a standing ovation were pivotal. Guidance: choosing or recognizing an audience that's 'with' the performer amplifies difficult material. Anti-pattern: performing to an audience that isn't emotionally aligned, which can undercut risky or vulnerable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability and emotional risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Notaro repeatedly nearly cried during the performance—"When I walked out and said, 'Hello, I have cancer,' my voice was shaky and I almost cried"—showing that exposing real emotion is part of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: visibly allowing emotion (shaky voice, tears) can deepen audience response and authenticity. Example: mixture of laughter and tears in the same set. Anti-pattern: suppressing emotion to the point of sterility, which can make personal stories feel less true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to perform / seizing the moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite recent diagnoses and crises, Notaro chose to do the scheduled show: she got the prognosis, was devastated, got a text about the show and replied simply, "Yes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: opting to perform in adverse circumstances can yield powerful, authentic material and moments that resonate. Example: the decision to keep the Largo date contributed to the set's impact. Anti-pattern: backing out of a performance that could produce meaningful work out of fear of vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective engagement with one's own recordings
rubrics_metrics.description: Notaro says, "I don't listen to it. I'm not a fan. I don't like listening to myself," and only listened once before release, suggesting a stance of limited self-review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: performers may choose not to obsessively re-listen to recordings and instead allow others to identify and amplify moments. Guidance: avoid over-analyzing recorded performances in ways that undercut spontaneity. Counterpoint: some artists do meticulous reviews; this is a personal preference rather than a universal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bluntness / confronting difficult truths
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene in the film recounts a doctor telling Notaro, "Sometimes in life we don't always get what we want," and Notaro says she "appreciated, actually, that she was confrontational"—valuing blunt clarity about stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: including blunt, confrontational language or scenes can clarify stakes and increase emotional weight. Example: the doctor's bluntness made the seriousness clear. Anti-pattern: softening or euphemizing critical facts so the audience underestimates consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resisting reductive labeling of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Notaro states, "I truly don't feel like a female comedian, I don't feel like a cancer comedian... I just feel like a comedian," indicating a criterion of not letting narrow labels define one's craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: avoid framing your work solely through a single identity or diagnosis; emphasize the craft first. Guidance: while identity-informed perspectives matter, letting labels be the defining feature may limit audience perception and artistic freedom. Example: embrace the role as comedian rather than a 'cancer comedian.'
